title: Behind the Scenes of AI Phone Calls: The Stand-In Was Human
part1:
If phone calls had cast lists, some of Muse’s tests might have listed “human contract workers.” The AI did not make the calls. Trained staff called people and completed the conversations. To use a stage metaphor, the lead stepped into the wings and a stand-in came on.

The key point in this story is not only that people stepped in to help. It is that the roles changed without users being properly told. Meta employees raised privacy concerns that sensitive user information needed to complete calls could be shared unintentionally with contract workers at a call center.
part2: But it is too soon to turn this into a “major data leak” story. What was raised was concern about the possibility that information could be shared, not a claim that a major leak had taken place. Still, if people take part in handling things without users knowing, more people may have access to their information. When you ask AI to take care of something, how much of your information is passed on, and to whom? That too is something to consider when choosing a service.
part3:
The vice president in charge of the relevant team at Meta admitted that it was a mistake to start tests in which contract workers made calls without proper disclosure, and put the human concierge feature on hold for now. The curtain came down only on that feature; Muse as a whole did not stop.

In the end, perhaps the main character in this scene was neither AI nor a person, but an explanation that clearly showed what was happening behind the scenes. It is not only whether the AI’s voice sounds natural, but also who actually makes the calls. Letting users know that is also an important part of helping them feel safe leaving it to the service.
in_one_line: Meta’s AI phone-call tests used human contractors instead, without properly informing users, so the feature was paused.
